text:
People find some episodes of an anime called frieren controversial because there is a race in it that are literally demons. powerful magical creatures that look like humans, but which are actually literally pure evil. like a Neutral Evil alignment, but to the nth degree. They want what they want, it seems to be domination, and they'll do literally anything to get it. They're pure machiavellians. Frieren exterminates them wherever she finds them, often because she reacts incorrectly to them and they try to murder her. She's also ancient, and demons know about her.  People are uncomfortable with a purely evil race, like a species that is absolutely Up To No Good by nature, and uncomfortable with a protag who would genocide them, and actively works towards it on occasion.

I think it's kind of funny. 1) the discomfort; 2) that there's a genocidal protag; 3) she's justified. It's like wiping out a sentient prion or something.

I appreciate that portraying Such A Thing is not exactly nice, nor a great lesson for people who use anime as a lesson (which i guess there are a lot of people, and my own Laws of Media state that simple production, reproduction, proliferation is enough of a rhetoric and people will use existence & ubiquity as pro arguments, consciously/unconsciously), however it's also nice to have, in a show that's about a character learning the nuances of humanity (she's an elf, portrayed as essentially an autistic, asexual waifu who examines you), a surprising little study on empathy for a japanese auty cartoon, the nuancedish portrait crashes against a creature or race with no nuance, who uses every studied nuance of humanity against it, to outright commit pure acts of sociopathy.

In short, I like that there's a race that's Pure Evil. I like the simplicity of it.

We see a lot of media that attempts to justify evil characters, nuance the evil away, or explain how they got that way. Not all, of course, I mean we still have Hannibal shit, etc., but even Silence of the Lambs makes Hannibal an interesting character that you almost sympathize with. Many movies make evil creatures that are Pure Evil to be disfigured monsters, orcs and goblins, spider things, oozes, etc. In this, you have a human-appearing set of creatures, elegant, intelligent, who are literally pure evil, from the outset. That's their motivation. And they should all be killed.

I am curious, as we move into a time that will see a proliferation of nonhuman actors that wear human faces, actors that may appear more or less intelligent while being more or less intelligent but perhaps programmed to or discovering on their own pure antipathies or motives that are directly antithetical to human flourishing, how we'll cope.

Anyway, I appreciate the simple portrait of pure evil because I like to see what an author thinks it looks like, and how they crash their portraits of good, or at least empathetic/sympathetic motives, against it.

text:
It was a dark, dark night.

Thom moved from memory; he could not see his feet, nor the room they carried him through. One hand out, he felt a bedframe, took three paces, a doorknob. Twist, open.

The next room was a little brighter. A pale light shone through drawn blinds, which he approached. Drawing them back, he encountered the Milky Way.

A dazzling tranche of stars blazed across a clear firmament. The ocean caught each, reflecting its image back into space, dancing quiet.

Thom considered this image in silence for ten seconds, then closed the curtains. He poured a glass of tap water, sipped it, then sat at his kitchen table.

Thom started thinking, but they weren't good thoughts, so he stopped. Then he wondered about the poor quality thoughts, and tried to produce some good ones, but they would not come. Thom wondered where the good thoughts had gone. If he was capable of producing any.

Thoughts probably come to you, rather than the other way around, he thought. Then he poured out his glass, and stood at the sink. His eyes were used to this light, but he preferred the total darkness. His air conditioning hummed. A drip of condensation. The drip warping his floor. Eating through, ruining his neighbor's ceiling. He couldn't decide if he cared. He was aware. But he didn't do anything about it. He didn't even report it. It didn't seem that his neighbor cared either.

Why was he thinking about that. He had such little time on Earth. He was thinking about a leaky pipe. That he actively repressed thoughts of. Every day. Actively considering repressing those thoughts. Considering the effort of repressing those thoughts. Considering how it all became too much when it was nothing at all.

The bathroom doorknob was falling off. He needed a new door, the holes in the door were wrong, nothing he could do. But this wasn't his space for long, he was leaving anyway. The kitchen sink drained slow. The furniture was not placed correctly. The bed hurt his back.

Thom decided to leave his apartment. After all, he'd rented the place for its location.

Thom put on pants, unbunched his boxers beneath them. Buckled his belt. Pulled a hoodie over his t-shirt, even though the air was just shy of amniotic. Breeze, he reasoned. He kicked on a pair of old shoes, the ones with the thinner soles, and walked out into the hall, patting his pockets for keys, wallet, cell phone, pen.

Why pen? He wasn't going to write at 12:30am on the beach.

Two pens.

He closed the door. Locked it. Checked the lock. Ambled down 3 sets of stairs. 

Wincing into a bright hallway, lights bleaching out the world around it. Out of the hallway, into the night, toward the beach.

The sound of the beach greeted him before his eyes adjusted. Thom never quite heard the beach from his apartment. It was a funny use of money, he worked all day, most days, right out of his apartment, and he could kind of see the beach from his windows, but usually kept the windows closed because he worked best in the cold and dark. He wondered if it was worth the money. One room is the same here as anywhere else. A day at the beach a week, though, that's a treat. But is it enough of a treat? What quantity of pleasure would justify the decision?

That's the question: am I getting enough out of paradise?

This is paradise, right?

Thom shook his head and looked up. The stars continued to look down on him. If possible, they had gotten brighter, the sky clearer. The atmosphere faded, and all of creation approached, more luminous, more sparkling. Palm trees just audible over a quiet ocean's whisper, light wind playing with the hair on his neck.

And what was the point of being in paradise if he wasn't making use of it. One day a week at a beach, did that merit uprooting his life here to this location, a place where he didn't know a soul, it wasn't really vacation, and maybe the pressure to be in paradise, to feel like he was making good use of paradise, that prevented a proper sense of paradise, what paradise was supposed to be for. I mean, what is paradise supposed to be for? Relaxation? Happiness? When was the last time he felt those things? It wasn't in paradise. Was it? A lot of pressure, paradise.

Thom walked onto the sand and removed his shoes. He wiggled his toes and dug them lightly into the beach, squeezing it underfoot, releasing it. The grains were powder-fine. Soft. Setting off across the shore, toward the water he tasted salt and a light memory of childhood played just beneath his conscious awareness such that he felt touched but uncertain of why.

After all if he couldn't relax here, what hope was there for him. Maybe he should have gotten an apartment in Topeka, Kansas. No pressure there, who gives a shit, right? Flat. Nothing to see. Literally, nothing to see. You can look out your window, see a flat horizon, or a neighbor's house, and feel no guilt for closing the blinds. It doesn't matter. Nothing in Topeka matters. Isn't that freedom? No guilt about being in paradise. But I'd resent it. Because I don't have to live in Topeka. And Topeka is fucking awful. Not that Thom's been to Topeka. It's an assumption. But it's what Topeka stands for. Flat. Charmless. A place you settle for.

The sand became wet. Waves rolled up and down the beach. Ocean touched his toes. An occasional shell found his soles, but nothing sharp. Smooth. It enhanced the soft sand. The water was warm, perfect counterpoint to the cool breeze. Where his feet dipped in, they stepped through stars. The small waves were lined with bioluminescent life, a startling blue glow underpinning the galaxy above.

And Thom wasn't settling. He wasn't in a place to settle. He'd broken up with his ex because he was not willing to settle. He took a chance on that girl who broke his heart because he was unwilling to settle. He kept moving because he was unwilling to settle. Hometown didn't cut it, so he jumped across the country. That didn't cut it, so he'd left the country. He was advancing in his job. Slowly, the work seemed to be paying off. But sometimes no settlement cost a lot of stress. There was a lot to learn and relearn in every new city, with every new woman. The locales and the people began to lose their spark. Each place kind of became another place. Probably because he was doing the same thing in each place. Which meant that the problems were really a him thing. But he knew that. But it's hard to change in the right direction when most things seem to be in a generally correct direction already, but the general sense of happiness doesn't improve. Thom thought about CBT, other forms of therapy, but something about that kind of self-brainwash didn't really sit right with him. He could talk to more people, go out more, but usually that just made him tired. He'd never really understood people. Like, what do you do with people? They hang around. They're in your space. You can talk to them, but when you're done what do you do? He liked people, but keeping them around was strange. He wanted them nearby, but in this vague way, not even for purposes, just to be close. But that kind of nearness, vague intentions, is a strange thing to confess. There was no fundamental ease to it. Was there supposed to be ease to it? It looked like there was a lot of ease to it for other people.

Thom withdrew from the water. It was not too cold. He found a beach chair from a hotel waterfront and sat on it. Private beaches were not guarded. The area was too nice. Slowly, a wave of color crept up from the horizon. All at once, brilliant shifting columns blazed across the sky in greens and blues and purples and pinks. The stars and the bioluminescence and the aurora all mixed in the ocean.

And all of this would be fine if he just weren't so tired all the time. Why was he always so tired? Thom had plenty of energy, but whenever he needed it for something practical, it was nowhere to be found. All the thoughts in the world but when he had to commit thinking to something worth money, worth the future, the mind was blank. It was as though Thom was not suited for practical function. Thom was a delicate and faulty mechanism, trying to achieve some perfect balance in a world infinitely askew. Thom rubbed his face, ran his fingers through his hair, his receding hairline, ran his fingers along his wrinkles, deeper and deeper. Was he wrong not to settle? He didn't have any regrets, he wasn't the type to have regrets, he was the type of person who appreciated who he was and who he was becoming but it's entirely possible he should have settled. But he couldn't have, because no one was right before. It's entirely possible that every ex belongs an ex, and he just might never meet the right one. And why should there be a Right One? These are fed narratives. He'd been brainwashed from youth to believe this. But why, then, was that the only attachment that felt properly meaningful to him? DID he need to brainwash himself? WERE the polyamorists right? Absolutely not. But then he had to choose between this deep constant aloofness and this absurd dig into everything is infinitely meaningful, falling in love with everyone at every moment. How was he supposed to function that way? Either way? Is it a choice between ennui or being blissed out? Or some kind of wife that will never come and the traditional struggles with that, men being from mars, women being from venus, and God laughing all the while.

The aurora intensified. Extremely vivid. Insanely vivid. The night had become a screaming, multicolored day. The ocean boiled with fish rising to the surface, jumping. Some beached themselves.

Thom wondered if it was a problem with self-worth. Who was he to believe he deserved the captive attentions of another. Every single person sitting in their air conditioned rooms, connected to the world only through their computers and their labor, staring at the beach 5 minutes a day and deciding it was enough. The morning coffee was enough time to appreciate paradise after all, then one had to get about the business of sustaining their position in paradise. It seemed the building was vibrating, as though the earth was shaking but at a very specific frequency. It was oddly soothing.

"Maybe the AirBnB was worth it after all."

Thom slid into a dream.

text:
Met a man at a tapas bar in Buenos Aires.

Sat down one seat's distance between him and I.

He heard me speak English. Asked me where I’m from.

Texas, I always say.

He’s flown in from Los Angeles.

But he was born in Buenos Aires.

Lived here until his 20s. Moved to LA.

Man had a habit of dropping hints about his life. Half-stories that would become relevant later as he talked about himself.

He’s from Buenos Aires. Had a choice to leave when he was young. Friends in Barcelona and LA. Figured moving to LA he’d at least learn English, whereas in Barca he’d learn nothing. Moved to LA to do freelance video work. Met a woman from Barca in Cali. Married her. Moved to Barca.

He described Barcelona as the biggest mistake of his life. Early aughts. Hatred of Castilian ran high at the time. He thought his Spanish would be an advantage. It fomented cultural estrangement. Intense isolation. He’d stopped video editing to do something stable for his family. Tried to make it work for 6 years. Couldn’t.

So his wife and he moved to São Paulo. Made sense. He knew Portuguese. She worked at international schools. They lived in a walled compound. Very nice compound. Everything paid for. But the city was insane. They tried to make it work for 4 more years. He was deeply unhappy. The marriage ended.

He moved back to LA. She moved to Kuala Lumpur with the kids.

He sees the kids every so often. I think they’re 12 and 16. He figures it’s good for them to live among Muslims, though both are baptized Catholic. They know Spanish, English. They’ll be culturally rich, have interesting experiences. He looks vacant when he says that. He misses his kids.

The tapas are good. I have a stack of fried calamari with potatoes and paprika. As is the custom in this country, before dinner you get a basket of bread with some kind of fresh vegetables marinated in oil, sometimes a light acid. This had lentils. Unexpected. Tasty.

My new friend had a large bowl of tripe. Callos. He'd not had the dish in many years. Deep pleasure lit him as he tried it. He ordered us both Fernet mixed with sparkling water. He wanted to see me try this strange drink. Delicious. Extremely bitter. Deep flavors. The mint plays over the top of the whole drink. Makes it excellent.

We talk for a while. Take a walk. There’s a bar somewhere. We should go to it.

We get lost. Take an uber. Bar’s closed. Walk until we find another bar.

The bar is small. We sit outside. The drinks are too sweet, but they’re strong. Strong enough to get the man talking again. About why he’s here.

It’s a woman.

Of course it’s a woman.

He shoots a wry look. Shows me a picture.

She’s cute. Of course she’s cute.

He met her on Facebook. Why not. The site suggested her to him. “People You May Know” or whatever. She was cute. He clicked on her. They started talking. It can be so simple.

They talked for a while. “E-dated.” It had been months. He wanted her to fly out to see him. She had a kid. Her whole life was in Buenos Aires. He bought a ticket to fly to her. He told her. She was excited.

A couple weeks prior to him flying out she went out dancing and fucked some other guy. She told him. His heart was torn out. Almost cancelled his ticket. He asked a friend what he should do. Friend said he should go to Buenos Aires anyway, but he shouldn’t see the woman.

He asked me what I thought. I told him he shouldn’t see the woman. He smiled. He said he’s seeing the woman tomorrow. I told him it will be a catastrophe. He said he knows she won’t be the one. She can’t be the one. Complications keep them apart. I tell him her behavior is literally crazy. She’s acting out to keep him from getting too close. He said he might not have sex with her. I tell him having sex with her would be a disaster. He smiles again.

I tell him I met my two great relationships online. I had a dysfunctional attachment to someone else I met online after. I’ve dated a few people between. I had experience in this arena. He should not talk to this person again. But the heart and the cock want what they want. I knew the man would not listen to me, a drunk, yelling stranger. I told him this too. He agreed.

We spent the rest of the night talking about music and drinking Quilmes.

We exchanged information. He’s on Instagram. Internationals love Instagram. I’ve followed some 50 instas after meetings just like this one, never talked to any of them again. raw.full_text:
Met a man at a tapas bar in Buenos Aires.

Sat down one seat's distance between him and I.

He heard me speak English. Asked me where I’m from.

Texas, I always say.

He’s flown in from Los Angeles.

But he was born in Buenos Aires.

Lived here until his 20s. Moved to LA.

Man had a habit of dropping hints about his life. Half-stories that would become relevant later as he talked about himself.

He’s from Buenos Aires. Had a choice to leave when he was young. Friends in Barcelona and LA. Figured moving to LA he’d at least learn English, whereas in Barca he’d learn nothing. Moved to LA to do freelance video work. Met a woman from Barca in Cali. Married her. Moved to Barca.

He described Barcelona as the biggest mistake of his life. Early aughts. Hatred of Castilian ran high at the time. He thought his Spanish would be an advantage. It fomented cultural estrangement. Intense isolation. He’d stopped video editing to do something stable for his family. Tried to make it work for 6 years. Couldn’t.

So his wife and he moved to São Paulo. Made sense. He knew Portuguese. She worked at international schools. They lived in a walled compound. Very nice compound. Everything paid for. But the city was insane. They tried to make it work for 4 more years. He was deeply unhappy. The marriage ended.

He moved back to LA. She moved to Kuala Lumpur with the kids.

He sees the kids every so often. I think they’re 12 and 16. He figures it’s good for them to live among Muslims, though both are baptized Catholic. They know Spanish, English. They’ll be culturally rich, have interesting experiences. He looks vacant when he says that. He misses his kids.

The tapas are good. I have a stack of fried calamari with potatoes and paprika. As is the custom in this country, before dinner you get a basket of bread with some kind of fresh vegetables marinated in oil, sometimes a light acid. This had lentils. Unexpected. Tasty.

My new friend had a large bowl of tripe. Callos. He'd not had the dish in many years. Deep pleasure lit him as he tried it. He ordered us both Fernet mixed with sparkling water. He wanted to see me try this strange drink. Delicious. Extremely bitter. Deep flavors. The mint plays over the top of the whole drink. Makes it excellent.

We talk for a while. Take a walk. There’s a bar somewhere. We should go to it.

We get lost. Take an uber. Bar’s closed. Walk until we find another bar.

The bar is small. We sit outside. The drinks are too sweet, but they’re strong. Strong enough to get the man talking again. About why he’s here.

It’s a woman.

Of course it’s a woman.

He shoots a wry look. Shows me a picture.

She’s cute. Of course she’s cute.

He met her on Facebook. Why not. The site suggested her to him. “People You May Know” or whatever. She was cute. He clicked on her. They started talking. It can be so simple.

They talked for a while. “E-dated.” It had been months. He wanted her to fly out to see him. She had a kid. Her whole life was in Buenos Aires. He bought a ticket to fly to her. He told her. She was excited.

A couple weeks prior to him flying out she went out dancing and fucked some other guy. She told him. His heart was torn out. Almost cancelled his ticket. He asked a friend what he should do. Friend said he should go to Buenos Aires anyway, but he shouldn’t see the woman.

He asked me what I thought. I told him he shouldn’t see the woman. He smiled. He said he’s seeing the woman tomorrow. I told him it will be a catastrophe. He said he knows she won’t be the one. She can’t be the one. Complications keep them apart. I tell him her behavior is literally crazy. She’s acting out to keep him from getting too close. He said he might not have sex with her. I tell him having sex with her would be a disaster. He smiles again.

I tell him I met my two great relationships online. I had a dysfunctional attachment to someone else I met online after. I’ve dated a few people between. I had experience in this arena. He should not talk to this person again. But the heart and the cock want what they want. I knew the man would not listen to me, a drunk, yelling stranger. I told him this too. He agreed.

We spent the rest of the night talking about music and drinking Quilmes.

We exchanged information. He’s on Instagram. Internationals love Instagram. I’ve followed some 50 instas after meetings just like this one, never talked to any of them again. But we go through the ceremony. I add his Instagram. He adds mine. We fist bump. Part ways. He walks off to his doom. Opening lips to a fresh hell he knows too well.

Buenas, amigo.

text:
An easy beginning, of ketamine haze and a shared bed, nothing serious but we slept together that first night and didn't spend a night apart for the next two weeks.

Casual intimacy easily gives way to something else, those conversations you have before you dream bridge into a picture we don't often share, not just for broader lack of interest, but for lack of time.

And it was comfortable to lavish that time on each other, something about the way you touched me or how I touched you, how our conversations fit between our angled heads, yours most often on my chest, mine straight up, pointed at the ceiling.

It grew out of very little, and the shape of our intimacy was explicitly bounded by what time we knew we had. But we didn't know we'd meet each other, and it grew from that chance conversation, initiated by curiosity, buoyed by attraction, into something neither of us expected, and which we both were loath to leave.

How can you expect these things? Even in expectation, they're impossible to Know until they happen. A person walks into your life, lays you down in their bed, and suddenly everything is different. You didn't know it would be them. You weren't sure it would happen again. You thought it might: there's a pattern now, you begin to suspect it will happen again. Still, every time is a surprise.

How did I meet you There, Then, and how did the nights become something more? Where was the border we tripped over, which would make you cry and have me reviewing little moments again and again?

Another couple weeks given to the past, an intimacy brewed in so specific an environment. What text can speak to it?

What have I to write to you? Written word feels so hollow compared to that little space, the small bed we overfilled.

This is why the poet works: confounded by plain speech, he knits feelings that cannot be stated into novelties. Explanation is not enough. The world must be recreated, and in the spaces between what is commonly understood and what the poet speaks into being, the reader can ideally approach God.

I, however, am no poet. I am a man in reflection, at the end of an illness.

And I'm reflecting on you still.

Sleep well.

text:
Within minutes of the Charlie Kirk shooting, memes were circulating about his death, shooting, the nature of the shooter, etc.

This is how an event is spread and digested: it is recorded in hundreds or millions of individual bits that are remixed and reassembled. 

However, a fair portion of what I saw was immediately and blatantly disrespectful, intended to ridicule Kirk, cause his memory harm, etc.

In a sufficiently diffuse and rapid social media environment, an extraordinary Incentive to Defect dominates what information is shared, and how it is shared.

I identify two main impulses here:
1) The Consolidating Impulse - the drive to unify information under existing norms or paradigms, to assimilate novel information into the structures that already typify the information environment. This has utility insofar as it attempts to preserve informational integrity and social cohesion, and there is obvious value in retaining and reinforcing extant structures. 
2) The Impulse to Defect - There is attention to be mined in defecting from extant norms/paradigms, and novelty, grotesquerie, and iconoclasm are accessible methods of expressing defection. Genuine disagreement can be simulated or expressed through the generation of memes or sentiments that contradict the consolidating impulse, and, regardless of how "good" a thing is, an attentional economy that emphasizes raw seconds mined will err towards incentivizing defection.

Almost 24 years ago to the day was September 11, 2001. National tragedy gripped America, and America's tragedy gripped much of the world. The destruction of The Towers and subsequent mourning, then rage periods were sacrosanct for years. It took not-long for conspiracy theories to develop, but these did not direct disrespect toward the event of 9/11 so much as they directed it toward the Bush Administration, the CIA, etc. People were cancelled for speaking out against the aggressions and wars we would prosecute after: in a notable case The Dixie Chicks, now just "The Chicks", talked shit about Bush and the impending 2003 Invasion of Iraq, and subsequently faced extraordinary backlash, from which their career never really recovered. This was a years-long respect cycle, through which public, meaningful defection was uncommon, and which ensured such defection would not be profitable, in the short term or the long term. Things have changed, obviously, and the sacred martyrs of WTC face nearly daily ridicule on T-shirts, hats, and in classic memes, but that took a little while to enter the public consciousness.

Assassinations and other violent events have frequently, in the past, been willfully charged with memetic meaning, both by the perpetrators, and by the viewers. Crassus was (supposedly) executed by having molten gold poured down his throat. Constantine (supposedly) had his soldiers paint the Chi-Rho on their shields. John Wilkes Booth (supposedly) screamed SIC SEMPER TYRANNIS after doming Abraham Lincoln. These are all attempts to charge actions with meaning that people can carry away from what might otherwise look to be a senseless act of violence. Suicide notes and manifestos are necessary accompaniments to major acts of human sacrifice.

Social media's acceleration of the informational environment, however, has decreased the time it takes for information to be taken from its source to mainstream awareness, democratized who gets to comment on it and whose opinions matter on a subject, and fundamentally fragmented the social fronts along which events carry their various meanings by commoditizing attention in manners previously impossible. This dramatically increases the incentive for the average person to defect from normative interpretations or behaviors as they seek to bear any new information with shocking relevance, carrying its memetic charge into the belly of their own community, or of a community they might create, and digesting it for clout.

The loop is tightened between the occurrence of an event and its ridicule, and nothing is sacrosanct because to a great many there is greater value in desecration.

text:
We rely too much on centralized methods of communication for news dispersal. Traditional media tries hiding violent or disagreeable content as quickly as it comes out, suppressing it algorithmically, manually or by rote.

I look for unfiltered content from an ongoing news story, say beatings in the Nepali revolution or a shooting, I want that content, regardless of the offense it causes some parties. I need primary sources to understand current events: it is my job, and understanding global mass movements is both a hobby and a civic necessity.

Common suppression of information via government pressure is constant and inimical, exerting a subtle or overt pressure to self-regulate speech in a way that soviet commissars would be envious of. And while our speech is broadly permitted within limits, it is just that, PERMITTED and WITHIN LIMITS. Our implements of speech must be more common, robust, and antifragile than resorting to X and Discord servers.

Because that's where I get my news. I used to scrape /pol/ after a Happening, but it became _fucking useless_ after the Christchurch shooting.

Obviously people are capable of circumventing any safeguards, and anyone who commits to a certain amount of research is capable of finding most of they want at the present. But those people are not common, and while it's probable that the knowledge gap is actually a-feature-not-a-bug in dictating information distribution, knowledge of how to do so will evaporate into the hands of specialists when Genuine Trouble occurs.

The production of our tech is massively centralized, and the apps we use for communication are massively centralized. It makes a man worry.

text:
Boredom. Discomfort with indolence to the point of itch, pain. To the point of manic pacing, up and down, noticing and noticing the same things. To the point of picking them up and putting them down, arranging and rearranging them. To the point of naming every thing, every single thing and trying to fit those things together. To the point of dismantling their names and deriving meaning from the phonemes, the letters, the syllables. To the point of disassembling the matter, tearing every atom from atom and the bits of the atoms apart.

To the point of naming every wave, sailing from one island to the next. To the point of having ten children who have ten children, whose children itch so bad they learn the stars and traverse great seas to greater lands. To the point where they name gods and stack rocks and build Babel and are thrown to the winds by the gods they named.

Itch. Itch. Itch.

The resource of itch. Of pain. The resource of disquiet.

text:
Two months out of my first long term relationship I was lonely, sad, and horny.

Tinder had blown up while I was in that relationship; I'd never used a dating app prior. So I made a profile, swiped around, and met with the minimum requisite amount of success.

Women responded. I set up a date with one.

"Date" is a glorified term for what really transpired. We agreed to meet at a Waffle House on the side of a highway. We sat at a table, had about 50 minutes of conversation and food, during which she ascertained that I was attractive enough, she was horny enough, and I wasn't super likely to murder her.

We got in our cars, I followed her to her place, and we sat on the sofa watching Seinfeld.

I'd actually never seen Seinfeld, so I probably spent more time watching it than she really wanted, but we got down to business, had a solid romp, did it again, and then she started to send me on my way, with the idea we'd probably meet again and do the same thing.

I got dressed, she was in a robe, one of those thin ones that shows off the form, she sat in a chair. Here I made a mistake.

I'd been in a relationship for the past 4.5 years. When this occurs, you get used to the particularities of a specific person, the way they kiss, the way they like to be kissed, and the way you want to kiss them when you feel certain ways. I'd seen literally no other girl for a bit over half a decade. And, reader, I was just following my heart.

I leaned in for a goodbye kiss, one deep one on the lips, and then, god help me, I kissed her forehead. I kissed it nice and domestic-like, in a way that surprised me, and her.

We didn't speak after that more than a "haha bye," but I felt an immediate vibe shift. I kinda knew I wouldn't see her again after that, something too much like love had been expressed where none was really intended or felt. Artifact of a dead relationship.

There's that sense that you need to fuck someone soon after the end of something meaningful to get over it. The only thing I find each every time I do this is actually I don't need to fuck somebody, and also I'm dragging my emotional aftershocks right into somebody else's sex life. Which, you know, yields really mixed results. For everyone involved.

Anyway, the moral of this story is while sex can be immediate, forehead kisses are for after marriage.

text:
Life becomes monotonous.

Much is about establishing a rhythm, a good rhythm or a functional rhythm at least.

Becoming a person who can beat a rhythm out of your environs, whatever is thrown at you, is important to becoming a strong person. But often any rhythm will do.

The addict loves his rhythm, as much as he hates it. The core of his days is owned by the rhythm of use, which he often times and ritualizes. It offers a certain future and a sense of the future. His shot will eat him, but he knows how he'll be eaten. The object of his addiction feels good, but the satisfaction of any activity grows to feel good on its own. The anticipation of the blade and its consummation with the flesh, each cut painful but a resolution of certain tension.

A person, in any situation, moves toward an equilibrium. A rhythm. His aptitude as a drummer varies, but it is human. Our heart tattoos one against our ribcage. Our breaths rise and fall with our actions.

The monotony is mandatory, though its degree varies. Our love or hate of it varies. But all things drive toward equilibrium. Toward rhythm.

And a proper excitement of the passions is an arhythmic disaster.

There's an old Zizek quote: "Love is a catastrophe. It's a crazy illness. Love ruins your life. But I am very sad when I am not [in] love."

You have a life. You have a pattern. You're doing something. Then a bolt hits you, product of a divine finger or a slow accretion, and nothing remains the same. Irrational compulsion seizes you, and whatever little pattern you were drumming out of your life is changed.

There's no choice in the matter. You've been had. And every love changes you, in its great and small ways. You're different now.

There's an alchemy to it. You can sense the beginnings of love. You can steer yourself away from it, a deliberate avoidance, but you're aware of a Gravity that steepens, and you fall. Feelings rise and flash, demand interpretation, move faster than you read them. Tea leaves and haruspicy. And if you don't read right, you're ruined.

And if you read right, fairly often you're ruined.

But I am very sad when I am not in love.

There is a kind of peace when you are not in love that you may try to preserve. A month or year out from the last Upset, you may find yourself actively avoiding it, or at least not courting it. You may feel perfectly fine. Good even. And then it strikes you, and whatever truth you were living prior seems so hollow, so false, that life is altered by matter of fact. You have to make Decisions.

The pains are extraordinary. You might not survive them. It might not even be worth it. But that feeling is so strong, it demands you try to make something of it. It feels so rich. Terribly pure. Thread of gold in your fraying rope.

I want to find an equilibrium woven with love. It might kill me, but I think I'm getting better at it with time. It seems that rhythm will defy me my whole life. But I think cleaving to that one energy makes sense, even as I run from it.

You're worth that catastrophe.

The pains are extraordinary. You might not survive them. It might not even be worth it. But that feeling is so strong, it demands you try to make something of it. It feels so rich. Terribly pure. Thread of gold in your fraying rope.

I want to find an equilibrium woven with love. It might kill me, but I think I'm getting better at it with time. It seems that rhythm will defy me my whole life. But I think cleaving to that one energy makes sense, even as I run from it.

You're worth that catastrophe.

That love changes can be terrifying, as all change can be. That something so firm and commanding and demanding as love shifts in form and requires you be responsive and change how you express it means your whole experience can shift in a moment, in ways you have little control over.

Learning how to love is a lifelong experience, fraught and arduous, but getting better at it permits such a warmth and depth of character. It's learning how to be a human, a better human, over and over.

Love is often overwhelming: it's at your core and your life changes around it, and the pain in a shift is your trajectory coming to terms with a fundamental alteration in how you carry the weight of your heart. But you don't really have a choice, do you? You have to love, or die. You have to carry on.

And if you're lucky, you get better at it.

text:
you're in a bad mood. you need to dissociate for a full week. why not binge cyberpunk 2077?

it's got everything: pretenses of depth that sometimes tip into real literary exploration, keanu reeves, beating androids to pieces with a massive hammer, a girlfriend simulator

the aesthetic of the game is exploration of the concept enough. it's artistically coherent and extremely well thought out in that regard.

the amount of scripting is exceptional too, even if it isn't great at times. the stories are fun, but the thing reads and sounds like a genx wet dream at times. the edgerunners show did an excellent job of sexing up the script and providing a concise run of the concepts the game sprawled through.

there's something particularly hamfisted about the relationship simulator in this one too. perhaps it's my current mental state, but you have your sexy genius engineer nomad queen who you can text little banalities to after you complete her storyline, and sometimes she shows up at your apartment where you can press x to cuddle press x to shower with her.

it's a funny element of a lot of games like this: immersion comes with performing specific actions that have very little bearing on the game itself, progressing the story or stats. you sit, you press a button to drink your whiskey, and you continue the conversation afterward with deliberate button presses. it feels like role playing role playing. imagining you're doing the thing by following the strict guidelines for the action.

the combat mechanics were pretty mid but once you get the literally titled "gorilla fists" and can literally bash a man's skull in with 1-3 blows, that's about half of the combat you're gonna have for the rest of the game, and it is viscerally satisfying.

i think the world of the game had more potential than the game mechanics permitted. everything quickly became classic missions, retrieving an item, escorting npcs, collecting stuff, etc. the puzzle elements felt underpowered, and while you can play the game with more a stealth or techy element, really you can put your fist through the whole game without suffering at all. that's fine, but my ethos is the sword of alexander is taken to every knot put before me.

anyway if you want to get drunk for a week that ends in a physical illness and just push through these quests it's an excellent distraction from processing whatever you're going through. proper disassociation fuel. 

back to books i think.

Wolfenstein: The New Order

The Nazis won WWII. You're a hulking maniac made of 300lbs of all-American red meat, transported to from 1946 to 1960 due to a head wound. You only talk in whispers, mumbled to yourself. You feel one emotion: Hatred of Nazis. Get to killing, bucko.

Honestly a perfect premise for a game but I'm having a hard time dissociating to it because it's actually hard. I refuse to play anything on "easy" or "medium" because I'm a masochist. I have spent hours slaughtering Nazis and their wretched robot ilk by this point. Saturday is fueled by rage and reheated buckets of Indian food. Every muscles in my body is tense. This distracts from some kind of dull ache in my chest, the tightness in my stomach forgotten next the tightness in my arms and neck from my raw seething hatred of Nazis and their horrible armored german shepherds.

text:
Winter in Montreal arrived with about a week of warning:

I was in autumn, wearing autumn clothes, walking around in cold but not frigid. The trees orange and red and yellow and the air good and then there was rain. For one week solid there was a rain and north of me was snow but was flirting with our little valley not quite touching the city, which was sodden but manageable.

The rain stopped, briefly, and we got one good day of blue, after which sky changed into that luminous impassive wall hanging heavy, that only says snow. And then, as promised, there was snow.

And there has not been a single day without snow since. And there will not be til May.

The temperature still hangs around 33F in the middle of the day. Things melt during the day and freeze at night. The sidewalks are still walkable between scrapings, and you can still get away with 3 layers on top if you have the right coat. But it's enough for me. I've entered hibernation.

My skin is the type of white that suggests I'd be well adapted to living in caves, that my ancestors would've treated the sun more a malevolent god than benefactor. But seasonal affective creeps in without direct knowledge, like a shifting climate. And the alcoholism of the Alaskans and Muscovites falls into place. In place of SSRIs and Vitamin D, hugging a bottle inside a cocoon makes sense.

But we're not doing that this year. We're rawdogging this unmitigated psychological disaster, one I somehow chose, and then fleeing just as it reaches its deepest state.

Perhaps, stepping off the plane from YUL to DFW, I'll find God.

Tonight the sky is orange. Enough snow and cloud has vanished to where I've taken a walk to say some final goodbye to Mile End before it's completely, irrecoverably blanketed and frozen.

Something funny about finishing a nomadic period exactly where I started: frozen under in Montreal, swearing I'd never do this thing again.

So goes the whole of my life.

text:
For 4 years I've travelled.

The longest I've been in a single location for the past decade was about a year and a quarter in Asheville, in a little duplex with my ex. The place was cheap, but still hard for me to afford. It had wood floors and a cherry tree out front. The tree was grafted, half-white, half-pink blooms wreathed it every spring, turning into cherries that the bears would come by and strip from its branches. We had a matter of days after the cherries ripened to get our fill before they were all taken. On days where the bears came, it was impossible to leave the house. The whole cul-de-sac was effectively paralyzed. Our neighbors would turn their car alarms on to no avail. We'd just stare out our windows and watch those bastards break half the branches of this beautiful tree.

The duplex was 2 bedroom, and carried a lot of my life. 3 bookcases, all mostly full. Unimaginable wealth at the time. A printer, two desks, the second seldom used as my ex preferred to work from bed. We inherited a Tempur-Pedic toward the end of our life together. I didn't love it, it absorbed too much motion. An uncanny feeling mattress that preferred you have sex elsewhere. A sofa and a fainting couch style chair whose faux-leather started to flake, lightly then aggressively, a pseudo-dandruff that caused some of the biggest fights in the late stage of our relationship.

A kitchen that I tear gassed accidentally the first time I cooked with habanero. The place I learned how to combat ants with Borax. To wage chemical warfare on wasps. Where I tried CBD joints and played Red Dead 2, and pressed up glasses against the wall with my ex so we could listen to our duplex neighbor get into another fight with another man while we grinned at each other.

The place where we had our final fights, where she convinced me to start drinking again and then resented me for it, the place where she got her new job and decided to go back to school, the place where I moved out of and into my manager's basement.

I'd lived in a duplex with her prior to that, some dinky carpeted place up an unpaved road, larger but shittier, darker. Prior to that I'd lived with my parents.

After the Asheville duplex I would not spent more than 10 months in a single location. Through this day. 2019.

I lived in the aforementioned basement. I lived in a room of a 3 story house in a very nice neighborhood back in Asheville. I've lived in 3 apartments in Montreal. A studio in Madrid that was more like a converted garage.

A vacation property in Larnaca, a beautiful little place in Sliema, an old building in Mexico City (whose age reassured me against my always-growing fear of an earthquake), a single room and then an apartment in Lisbon, a single room in Florence, a nice place in Buenos Aires, a place that felt like a converted hallway in Montevideo, another studio in Porto.

And now I sit in Montreal, in Mile End, listening to the wind sweep brutally across a lightly snow-dusted outdoors, frozen although it is above freezing, as the landscape sinks into a deep freeze it will not come out of til April, just after the longest night of the year.

In a week I fly to Porto again to rave with my Euros over the New Year. A week (?) after I fly to Texas to spend time with my family, about a month I'd guess.

And then I fly to New York City to try to stay in a single location for at least a year.

That will be a very real accomplishment for me, geographic stability for 12 months. You'll know I've Made It if I have both my 35th and 36th birthdays in the same location.

Every single place I've stayed becomes a time capsule for a portion of my life. I have this habit that I keep up with more and less well: when I enter a new space I'll be living in, I like to photograph it prior to my fully moving in, then again at its peak mess, who it looks like when fully broken in, lived-in. Each location is so distinct a container for the memories I constructed there that I recall the rooms of each place when I want to remember what life was like for that time.

I can usually remember even the hotel rooms I occupied. The quirks of the showers and toilets. The positions I ate in, worked in. The meals I became autistically devoted to over the course of my stay.

That geospatial sense contains the greater part of my memory, the containers within which my life was lived, and how I moved through them. I can remember the shape of my life, and it answers some of the whys, why I was that person for that time, how and who.

raw.full_text:
For 4 years I've travelled.

The longest I've been in a single location for the past decade was about a year and a quarter in Asheville, in a little duplex with my ex. The place was cheap, but still hard for me to afford. It had wood floors and a cherry tree out front. The tree was grafted, half-white, half-pink blooms wreathed it every spring, turning into cherries that the bears would come by and strip from its branches. We had a matter of days after the cherries ripened to get our fill before they were all taken. On days where the bears came, it was impossible to leave the house. The whole cul-de-sac was effectively paralyzed. Our neighbors would turn their car alarms on to no avail. We'd just stare out our windows and watch those bastards break half the branches of this beautiful tree.

The duplex was 2 bedroom, and carried a lot of my life. 3 bookcases, all mostly full. Unimaginable wealth at the time. A printer, two desks, the second seldom used as my ex preferred to work from bed. We inherited a Tempur-Pedic toward the end of our life together. I didn't love it, it absorbed too much motion. An uncanny feeling mattress that preferred you have sex elsewhere. A sofa and a fainting couch style chair whose faux-leather started to flake, lightly then aggressively, a pseudo-dandruff that caused some of the biggest fights in the late stage of our relationship.

A kitchen that I tear gassed accidentally the first time I cooked with habanero. The place I learned how to combat ants with Borax. To wage chemical warfare on wasps. Where I tried CBD joints and played Red Dead 2, and pressed up glasses against the wall with my ex so we could listen to our duplex neighbor get into another fight with another man while we grinned at each other.

The place where we had our final fights, where she convinced me to start drinking again and then resented me for it, the place where she got her new job and decided to go back to school, the place where I moved out of and into my manager's basement.

I'd lived in a duplex with her prior to that, some dinky carpeted place up an unpaved road, larger but shittier, darker. Prior to that I'd lived with my parents.

After the Asheville duplex I would not spent more than 10 months in a single location. Through this day. 2019.

I lived in the aforementioned basement. I lived in a room of a 3 story house in a very nice neighborhood back in Asheville. I've lived in 3 apartments in Montreal. A studio in Madrid that was more like a converted garage.

A vacation property in Larnaca, a beautiful little place in Sliema, an old building in Mexico City (whose age reassured me against my always-growing fear of an earthquake), a single room and then an apartment in Lisbon, a single room in Florence, a nice place in Buenos Aires, a place that felt like a converted hallway in Montevideo, another studio in Porto.

And now I sit in Montreal, in Mile End, listening to the wind sweep brutally across a lightly snow-dusted outdoors, frozen although it is above freezing, as the landscape sinks into a deep freeze it will not come out of til April, just after the longest night of the year.

In a week I fly to Porto again to rave with my Euros over the New Year. A week (?) after I fly to Texas to spend time with my family, about a month I'd guess.

And then I fly to New York City to try to stay in a single location for at least a year.

That will be a very real accomplishment for me, geographic stability for 12 months. You'll know I've Made It if I have both my 35th and 36th birthdays in the same location.

Every single place I've stayed becomes a time capsule for a portion of my life. I have this habit that I keep up with more and less well: when I enter a new space I'll be living in, I like to photograph it prior to my fully moving in, then again at its peak mess, who it looks like when fully broken in, lived-in. Each location is so distinct a container for the memories I constructed there that I recall the rooms of each place when I want to remember what life was like for that time.

I can usually remember even the hotel rooms I occupied. The quirks of the showers and toilets. The positions I ate in, worked in. The meals I became autistically devoted to over the course of my stay.

That geospatial sense contains the greater part of my memory, the containers within which my life was lived, and how I moved through them. I can remember the shape of my life, and it answers some of the whys, why I was that person for that time, how and who.

A little under two months, and the nomading is over.

Supposedly.

I won't believe it til I get there.

And New York doesn't feel like the place where I'm going to settle. Something dramatic will have to convince me.

See you soon.

text:
Part of what I mean by the classical writing and regimentation is how explicitly Wes Anderson lays out his productions. If you've ever read a play, it starts by explaining and listing all the characters, then goes about progressing through different explicitly laid acts.

Anderson treats the film as the extended stage of a play. I believe in Moonrise Kingdom, he starts the film off with a vinyl that explains the composition of a classical song, and then likens the characters to pieces of an orchestra, then puts his characters through the various movements in a symphony.

That's how he thinks of everything: very well-organized, in parts that are explicit, so explicit you often see the ribs, the bones of a work, and yet it's often more lovely for it. Asteroid City, which I've not yet finished, is perhaps the most explicitly laid out version of this he's produced, however the recent Netflix Shorts he produced (The Wonderful World of Henry Sugar, et al.) were very obviously constructed as stage productions, and beautifully so, it contributed to their fluidity.

I only bring this up to continue to justify my likening to Sufjan, who is clearly a classically trained composer and instrumentalist constructing explicitly and well-laid songs to express deep emotional truths in a deeply American manner.

I say American for Anderson because, regardless of the characters he's producing there's a brash energy to them. Protagonism is about bright individuals who thrust themselves forward against odds and issues, and through inventiveness, perseverance, and good honest self-expression achieve what they intend (how he starts out is Rushmore, for God's sake!).

text:
Avatar III: How to Stop Worrying and Love the Spectacle

Last night Tim arrived at my house at 9:30PM. We formulated a plan: Rip plenty of that fine Canadian Green then uber to the Scotiabank Cineplex to watch Avatar III in IMAX 3D.

I don't smoke much weed, but they sell some of this good good that got me neuroticizing my entire life for an hour then chillin into deranged optimism that I cannot trust. I love it.

Anyway we arrive. This cineplex is 4 stories. Used to frequent it when I lived in Griffintown, because that's how a thing is: I go when it's proximal and it almost doesn't exist when it's not. Last night about half of the escalators were not running. We bought 2 tickets, popcorn, beverages, walked up 4 flights of stairs then retreated one, and made it to this massive theater with 10 people max inside it.

To begin with, previews. I was high, so I only remember one. The trailer for the new "The Odyssey." I remember it because it was not a trailer, it was a 10 minute chunk of the film's climax, which was stupefying spectacle. They gave away the best part of the film, I assume so that you'd be like "whoa well what the fuck is the context" or "whoa if that's what the preview is I wonder what else the film is" but those who know know.

The film starts without much warning, you're thrown into a friendly chase scene.

Guys, I don't remember much of the plot, but that's essentially the whole movie. Things happen, and then more things happen. There are like 10 storylines that are happening concurrently; the movie constantly trades off between them. Each is designed to be somewhat relatable to some demographic, there is a fairy nature gaia teen played by a mid-70s Sigourney Weaver, daddy who is gruff but only because he cares for his family so so much and he needs to be because the world is brutal, children all trying to prove themselves to the family, a mom from a different culture who is trying to internalize the differences between these demi-human creatures she's brought into the world from her own native na'vi. An evil man who is trying to reach out to his human son and thereby might find redemption. A goofy human sidekick whose role is to always be almost dying but whose heart is In It. Forbidden lovers. On and on. At some point, Cameron is trying to ensure everyone is represented, so that even if you're bored with the "oh shit gaia teen figured out how to breathe under water using fairy wing biotechnology" there will soon be blood.

And that's what Cameron's good at: moving plot. Even if half of the occurrences in the film are technically coincidence, they happen so frequently and rapidly that you just kind of accept things as they move forward through 3 hours and 15 minutes of weaving. The movie moves because almost constantly the characters move. Pretty often the ground is literally unstable beneath those characters.

A little aside, Cameron's vision frequently reminded me of Paul Gauguin. Something about his idealization of these culturally untouched natives who wander around with all their skin out, sanitized by touches like tits without nipples as though the removal of the functional bit desexualizes them when it's quite the opposite, there's all the form of sex but no funciton, kind of a hilarious bit. Like, Cameron wants to fuck the na'vi. I know this.

Anyway the movie is acceptable. Plot-wise, this is the weakest of the 3 released films so far. The only truly interesting character to me is the main Villain and his bad bitch. The protagonist family that we follow is an exercise in constant trauma bonding with storylines that I didn't care much about because they always resolve the same way, "we are a family and family is stronger than everything, and let's unite the tribe(s)." The villain is genuinely murderous, and the real unbelievable aspect about him is that he cares for his goofy human boy whose main role in the film is to be like "whoa tight" when some na'vi magic is pulled, or to just almost die a lot and kinda get in the way. Fuck that kid. Fuck Spider. The villain has a blood vs soil thing going on, you don't know how much he's growing, but he's genuinely on his own path, and in a compellingly murderous way. Aite.

The main takeaway for me, though, is the spectacle of the film.

The theater was large and empty, and the way Avatar was "shot" and screened involved a lot of very specialized equipment that I assume is expensive, relatively rare, and becoming rarer as the cinema in general dies.

But the experience of seeing a film on a massive screen with those enormous speakers is a completely distinct experience from watching at home, or via VR. It's a way to be dominated. I haven't watched a film without distraction taking me away from it every 5 minutes in a year or so, and, u'know, "skill issue," however something about the sheer scale of the screen, the pace of the film, and the loudness of the speakers beat me into submission. It is a distinct experience.

And that's exactly what Cameron is both aiming for and gifted at producing: Spectacle. This film, all these films, are raw spectacle. There's tremendous detail in every shot, and the shots come rapidly. They're imaginative. And they're huge.

Huge. They take the whole wall, every inch is used for some magical bioluminescent or otherwise shiny object, imagined and executed from end to end with some attention. It reminds me of art class in like 4th grade when I would draw something small in the off-center of a page and the teacher would come up and encourage me to "use the whole page." Cameron fuckin loves using the whole page.

But there's something to these massive temples of spectacle that will likely go the way of the mall. All these centralized, monumental hubs devoted to some manner of human congress are expensive, and their margins are thinner than when selling a download to a human sitting in front of their $400, 55" screen. And the massive, obsessively choreographed spectacle is precisely what this genre is, without a true Big Screen it loses a fair amount of its impact.

So, in summary: plot's a bit mid in this one, hit or miss at times, but i see Cameron's vision toward making something truly universal that people will be able to find relevance to for years for its raw spectacular appeal and broadly relatable plotting. Avatar III: How to Stop Worrying and Love the Spectacle

Last night Tim arrived at my house at 9:30PM. We formulated a plan: Rip plenty of that fine Canadian Green then uber to the Scotiabank Cineplex to watch Avatar III in IMAX 3D.

I don't smoke much weed, but they sell some of this good good that got me neuroticizing my entire life for an hour then chillin into deranged optimism that I cannot trust. I love it.

Anyway we arrive. This cineplex is 4 stories. Used to frequent it when I lived in Griffintown, because that's how a thing is: I go when it's proximal and it almost doesn't exist when it's not. Last night about half of the escalators were not running. We bought 2 tickets, popcorn, beverages, walked up 4 flights of stairs then retreated one, and made it to this massive theater with 10 people max inside it.

To begin with, previews. I was high, so I only remember one. The trailer for the new "The Odyssey." I remember it because it was not a trailer, it was a 10 minute chunk of the film's climax, which was stupefying spectacle. They gave away the best part of the film, I assume so that you'd be like "whoa well what the fuck is the context" or "whoa if that's what the preview is I wonder what else the film is" but those who know know.

The film starts without much warning, you're thrown into a friendly chase scene.

Guys, I don't remember much of the plot, but that's essentially the whole movie. Things happen, and then more things happen. There are like 10 storylines that are happening concurrently; the movie constantly trades off between them. Each is designed to be somewhat relatable to some demographic, there is a fairy nature gaia teen played by a mid-70s Sigourney Weaver, daddy who is gruff but only because he cares for his family so so much and he needs to be because the world is brutal, children all trying to prove themselves to the family, a mom from a different culture who is trying to internalize the differences between these demi-human creatures she's brought into the world from her own native na'vi. An evil man who is trying to reach out to his human son and thereby might find redemption. A goofy human sidekick whose role is to always be almost dying but whose heart is In It. Forbidden lovers. On and on. At some point, Cameron is trying to ensure everyone is represented, so that even if you're bored with the "oh shit gaia teen figured out how to breathe under water using fairy wing biotechnology" there will soon be blood.

And that's what Cameron's good at: moving plot. Even if half of the occurrences in the film are technically coincidence, they happen so frequently and rapidly that you just kind of accept things as they move forward through 3 hours and 15 minutes of weaving. The movie moves because almost constantly the characters move. Pretty often the ground is literally unstable beneath those characters.

A little aside, Cameron's vision frequently reminded me of Paul Gauguin. Something about his idealization of these culturally untouched natives who wander around with all their skin out, sanitized by touches like tits without nipples as though the removal of the functional bit desexualizes them when it's quite the opposite, there's all the form of sex but no funciton, kind of a hilarious bit. Like, Cameron wants to fuck the na'vi. I know this.

Anyway the movie is acceptable. Plot-wise, this is the weakest of the 3 released films so far. The only truly interesting character to me is the main Villain and his bad bitch. The protagonist family that we follow is an exercise in constant trauma bonding with storylines that I didn't care much about because they always resolve the same way, "we are a family and family is stronger than everything, and let's unite the tribe(s)." The villain is genuinely murderous, and the real unbelievable aspect about him is that he cares for his goofy human boy whose main role in the film is to be like "whoa tight" when some na'vi magic is pulled, or to just almost die a lot and kinda get in the way. Fuck that kid. Fuck Spider. The villain has a blood vs soil thing going on, you don't know how much he's growing, but he's genuinely on his own path, and in a compellingly murderous way. Aite.

The main takeaway for me, though, is the spectacle of the film.

The theater was large and empty, and the way Avatar was "shot" and screened involved a lot of very specialized equipment that I assume is expensive, relatively rare, and becoming rarer as the cinema in general dies.

But the experience of seeing a film on a massive screen with those enormous speakers is a completely distinct experience from watching at home, or via VR. It's a way to be dominated. I haven't watched a film without distraction taking me away from it every 5 minutes in a year or so, and, u'know, "skill issue," however something about the sheer scale of the screen, the pace of the film, and the loudness of the speakers beat me into submission. It is a distinct experience.

And that's exactly what Cameron is both aiming for and gifted at producing: Spectacle. This film, all these films, are raw spectacle. There's tremendous detail in every shot, and the shots come rapidly. They're imaginative. And they're huge.

Huge. They take the whole wall, every inch is used for some magical bioluminescent or otherwise shiny object, imagined and executed from end to end with some attention. It reminds me of art class in like 4th grade when I would draw something small in the off-center of a page and the teacher would come up and encourage me to "use the whole page." Cameron fuckin loves using the whole page.

But there's something to these massive temples of spectacle that will likely go the way of the mall. All these centralized, monumental hubs devoted to some manner of human congress are expensive, and their margins are thinner than when selling a download to a human sitting in front of their $400, 55" screen. And the massive, obsessively choreographed spectacle is precisely what this genre is, without a true Big Screen it loses a fair amount of its impact.

I've never lived in NYC before. Only been through 3 times, each completely different.  Excited to see who I see, meet who I meet, and learn whatever is in store for me in this new arc.

See you soon.

text:
The path is narrow.

My new home is one long hallway with 3 a couple chambers on the side. There are few lights. Bedroom to kitchen to bathroom to front door in one line. Straight from my door to the front of the apartment building. I'm on the first floor.

I take a left. I walk straight. There is an intersection. Immediately on the other side is my train. 11 stops on the F. One right, one left. A few blocks. I'm at my office.

Office door to chair. Behind two monitors and a laptop. Seat to kitchen for snacks to seat to bathroom to seat to bathroom to seat to kitchen to seat to bathroom. 8-10 hours of vexations.

I leave. Gym is one block away. Cardio. 30 minutes going nowhere. Lift weight put down. Shower. Subway near. 11 stops. Home. The long hallway. It's dark. I can't sleep. The magnesium doesn't help. Drugs don't help. Harder drugs don't help. I fall asleep. I wake up. Too soon. 30 minutes to become a human. Repeat.

Narrow halls. Try not to talk to strangers. Keep your noise cancellers clamped around your skull. It's loud out there. Narrow cars. Dirty pavement. Public surfaces. A toothless man whose feet are falling off. A rainbow spread over undrinkable water. A pigeon that talks shit at you. A smiling baby and a frowning mother. Ten thousand problems. Marginal impact. Wrapped up in my coat. 2 hoods up. Maybe a hat. No eye contact. A smile by accident. A screen to deflect. 

The path is narrow.

text:
Seinen anime frequently centers on finding/building a family in an eternally shifting world where nothing is granted.

Evangelion, Chainsaw Man, Cowboy Bebop, Berserk, Devilman Crybaby, etc.

Each described, and many others, features characters coming from a hard situation in a prior life, finding solace in the individuals they wind up with, and trying to build a family where they are. Frequently this still ends in disaster.

In most, the happiness characters temporarily acquire in their found family situations serves to hilight the tragedy of their lives and the ultimate loss of those situations. Nothing good was provided by society, and when whatever seems good in life is ostensibly yielded through extraordinary efforts and kismet, it is wrenched away.

Shonen usually don't last that long: they're about kids learning to struggle, finding those families, and hewing to them against all odds to build a better future, and a better life. That quite often works out, and everyone is better off for it.

The bleakness of the Seinen situations, where whatever hope exists only exists to perpetuate and ultimately deepen suffering, speaks to general sense of life gone on too long without a strong core or a fulfillment of the social contract. It is nihilism, defeated only by a persistence often, and rightly, portrayed as insanity.

our plan: meet, drop off an excessive order of the powder in my room, pocket enough for an adventure, and then launch out

and we did.

arriving at the museum itself was a trip. there were many, many children. new york is a crowded city, full of people and things, many of them loud, demanding attention. we checked our coats, walked up a floor, and insufflated, then meandered out to be immediately confronted with a vast horde of children focused on a novel art display, messing about with colorful implements, parents and guardians dispersed among them to maintain a type of control.

there's something about skipping out on your degenerate finance gambling job to rail ketamine in the bathroom at the moma in new york that makes you feel a little weird about being around children, but i think we managed composure.

getting your stilty tree trunk legs to carry you a to b is the main preoccupation for certain bits of your trek, but it's appropriate, it's fun to have to pay attention to the little shuffles you usually dart through unthinking. the average movement becomes an unhinged dance, and interfacing with children means infinite unpredictable scintillations sliding around you while you attempt to present the type of wholesome facade that will be supportive of a good childhood, or an ignorable moment in childhood, or at least not a traumatic monument in the child's firmament

anyway

we got past those kids to a room full of more kids with giant steel blocks in four stacks. they were kinda cool. there's this era of modern american art where everyone was trying to make a monolith out of The Cube or really fixated on generating massive but simple forms and just splatting them out in public, calling it genius, and i guess it's a sort of genius, like the pharaohs converged around imhotep for his magnificent polyhedron, we have been doing it for as long as we have been Doing It, but the main use of that room was a bunch of essentially rubberized pillows in the shape of building blocks, which were pretty cool, which a bunch of the kids were playing with, which when we tried playing with them we were chastened by a very kindly twenty something who said the toys are for the children not realizing that me me me i am the children but oh well

so there was a hasty evacuation into a chamber full of plastic sheets with three projectors designed to engage in some kind of play with the new york skyline that was totally lacking and my friend and i were feeling a little catastrophic about the whole thing so we meandered away from these mid happenings and she had the correct notion to engage with a map for a sense of what we might actually want to happen in our shared future and i wanted old art which is a tragically ironic turn for someone who explicitly chose the metropolitan museum of modern art but bad art is bad come on and jesus christ we had to get away from the kids and the ten thousand voices so we ascended to the top floor and had a much better time

after slotting ourselves in and out of the bathroom there for another bump we meandered the surrealists and the modernists. there are mondrians and pollocks and picassos and miros and a surprising number of rothkos and a wyeth (who i am enamored with) and a couple of actually really great hoppers and i realize for the ten billionth time that i like these darker more dramatic more slashing forms of image and then my friend stops in her tracks when we stumble onto the monets and says we must do another bump and then specifically admire the lillys and i say yeah you know what that's exactly right and so we beat a hasty retreat to our respective stalls for a solitary sniff

now ostensibly ketamine should all be ketamine because it's a chemical a substance it should be one molecule it should hit one way and that should be that but actually there are isomers and impurities and whatever and i want to preface this next part by explaining that whatever we were jamming up our lovely holes was a truly blessed distillation of this glorious molecule that provides a platonic experience, a pillowy pinkpurple that carries you floatingly along while you merely observe the happenings around you. lovely, unique substance, which i am not at all underappreciating, and anticipate never quite getting my hands on this varietal again so almost why even bother but again this is a digression

so we horf our powders and while i get distracted she is very much focused so we make it right back to the monets and seize a whole little sofa thing and get to just sit and stare at these canvasses for like 20 minutes and i swear to you it was in that time impossible to be bored. gazing into the depths of those works, you see colors shifting as he saw them, things bleed into one another in ways that cannot be verbally conveyed, every single inch of these massive works is a delicate expression of shifting light and hue, the complexity of a single knot of color grants such a breadth of this man's experiences that you just sigh and know you're looking at the work of a genius who Really Saw God and managed to splatter the concept across our collective experience in a snapshot of grace

so for about 20 minutes there was peace

it's funny in these rooms with monumental works, truly famous works, you get to see such a scope of human behavior, parents showing children, girls taking pictures of each other wearing their most fashionable pouts, varying moments of reverence or uncaringness, a guy kisses his girlfriend, points and murmurs, gasps and coughs, chuckles, stomps, seats, humans humans humans

and there was my peace. getting lost in the colors of the work. and then observing others observe. my little joys.

at some point enough was had, and we made a cursory surveyance of what in the room we'd not stared at so ardently, then left. shortly after that, it was decided that we ought leave the museum altogether. yes there were warhols (she doesn't like him), and x and y but it's time to leave and you know what yeah actually it was time to leave

so we found a bathroom again sniffed a little more and left but it was still bright outside, the sky blue brilliant and very awake and the city very ardently calling our name so we walked and we walked and we walked.

there's something stupefying about nyc, like the scale of every individual building is so insane, and there are so god damned many of them, and everything is so absurdly expensive, and so many hands and eyes and feet have traversed every single square inch, it's that literally nothing around you has escaped the gaze of civilization. in the press and ferment of that city, everything is preserved, it is all known, and leaving a mark there is somehow to be known, to shape the little paths a million million feet take on a million million different days, the conversations echo differently in your halls, in these shared halls. it's all private and it's all public, everything spills out, boundaries are so jarring when you're pressed up against them necessarily, by virtue of so little space. you either tense up shrink and die or explode into some caricature of a person that approximates the humanity you're trying to claw back from the pressing eyes and ears and mouths and filth and walls.

so i'm high but in this simpleminded way and just kind of floatly about everything and my friend and i are chattering away about the buildings because that's the environment that's the whole world buildings and pavement, and she fixates on a building that's totally covered for renovation but the cover is made to look like louis vuitton luggage. there is a building right next to central park that looks like a pile of luggage. you can go see it now. for her it was this sensation of the luggage being so real looking, but unreal looking, but also so totally unignorably present, just this absurd monument in the middle of the city. we eventually got her away from it, but she was astounded.

the rest of the day was the most of it, but what's to be written?

we walked. we walked and walked and walked. and talked and talked and talked. there was no direction. we dipped into a shop every now and again, got a beverage, or some food, found a bathroom, did a bump, and kept up the meander.

in that way we floated through manhattan. the absurd thing about this city is when you wander, wherever you go you will always find something that demands attention. yes, that is the tunisian consulate. yes that is the fucking UN building i guess. yes this is a staircase with softly rutted stones from millions' feet passing. every single thing is monumental, can be recognized, demands recognition.

The rest of the evening was pleasant and simple. We ate in some strange food court. Saw the Rockefeller Center, astounded at the JPMorgan Chase building, like truly astounded at that building, something so bizarre about seeing a brand new landmark planted dead in the center of an island full of them, had zero proof drinks at a bar called the horny ram, we walked and walked and walked and walked.

but i can't quite shake that eve of apocalypse feeling.

everywhere i go lately i feel like i'm one of the first christians, the end is nigh the end is nigh, and i can't quite decide if anything i do really matters. i feel like i'm scheduling events for some point after the meteor hits. predicating all my todays on false tomorrows.

so we split and now i'm in my hotel room spraying this all over my keyboard. Hallelujah.
